'''Theodore Harold Maiman''' (July 11, 1927 – May 5, 2007) was an American engineer and [[physicist]] who is widely credited with the invention of the [[laser]].<ref name="Lengyel">{{Cite book |first=Bela A. |last=Lengyel |title=Lasers: Generation of Light by Stimulated Emission |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=1962 |pages=22–28 }}</ref><ref name="Bromberg">{{Cite book |last=Bromberg |first=Joan Lisa |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P6Ta1MPiOM8C&pg=PA86 |title=The Laser in America, 1950–1970 |publisher=MIT Press |year=1991 |pages=86–92 |isbn=978-0-262-02318-4 }}</ref><ref name="Bertolotti">{{Cite book |first=Mario |last=Bertolotti |title=The History of the Laser |publisher=Institute of Physics Publishing |year=2005 |isbn=0750309113 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/historyoflaser0000bert/page/226 226–234] |url=https://archive.org/details/historyoflaser0000bert/page/226 }}</ref><ref name="Townes">{{Cite web |first=Charles H. |last=Townes |title=The First Laser |website=A Century of Nature: Twenty-One Discoveries that Changed Science and the World|editor=[[Laura Garwin]] and Tim Lincoln |publisher=University of Chicago Press|year=2003|pages=107–12|url=http://www.press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/284158_townes.html}}</ref><ref name="Hecht">{{Cite book|first=Jeff|last=Hecht|title=Beam: The Race to Make the Laser|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2005|pages=106–15, 169–82}}</ref><ref name="Johnson">Johnson, John Jr. (May 11, 2008). "Theodore H. Maiman, at age 32; scientist created the first LASER". ''Los Angeles Times''</ref><ref name="History">{{Cite web|website=Physics History: May 16, 1960|title=Maiman Builds First Working Laser |date=May 2010 |publisher=APS News 19 |url=http://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/201005/physicshistory.cfm}}</ref> Maiman's laser led to the subsequent development of many other types of lasers.<ref name="LaserFest">{{Cite web|title=The First Ruby Laser|publisher=LaserFest|url=http://www.laserfest.org/lasers/how/ruby.cfm|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref><ref name="Voilá">{{Cite web|title=Voila. That was it! The Laser was born! Celebrating 50 Years of Laser Technology, 1960–2010|publisher=HRL Laboratories LLC|url=http://www.hrl.com/lasers/lsr_laser.html|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref> The laser was successfully fired on May 16, 1960. In a July 7, 1960, press conference in Manhattan,<ref name="Martin" /> Maiman and his employer, [[Hughes Aircraft Company]], announced the laser to the world.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hrl.com/lasers/pdfs/maiman_60.07.07.pdf|title=Speech by Dr. Theodore H. Maiman, Hughes Aircraft Company, at a Press Conference at the Hotel Delmonico|location=New York|date=July 7, 1960|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref> Maiman was granted a patent for his invention,<ref name="laserpatent">Maiman, Theodore H. (1961) "Ruby laser systems " {{US patent|3353115}}</ref> and he received many awards and honors for his work. His experiences in developing the first laser and subsequent related events are recounted in his book, ''The Laser Odyssey'',<ref name="Maiman1">{{Cite book|first=Theodore H.|last=Maiman|title=The Laser Odyssey|publisher=Laser Press|year=2000|isbn=978-0-9702927-0-4|url=http://www.laser-inventor.com|access-date=September 29, 2025}}</ref> later being republished in 2018 under a new title, ''The Laser Inventor: Memoirs of Theodore H. Maiman''.<ref name="MaimanS">{{Cite book|first=Theodore H. |last=Maiman |title=The Laser Inventor: Memoirs of Theodore H. Maiman |publisher=Springer |date=2018 |isbn=978-3-319-61939-2 |url=https://springer.com/gp/book/9783319619392 |access-date=July 9, 2020}}</ref>

==Early and student life==
[[File:Maiman with his father Abe.jpg|thumb|left|Maiman and his father Abe]]
Maiman was born in Los Angeles to a Jewish family, Abraham "Abe" Maiman, an electrical engineer<ref name="Martin" /> and inventor, and Rose Abramson. At a young age his family moved to [[Denver]], Colorado, where he helped his father with experimentation in a home [[electronics]] laboratory. Maiman says in his autobiography that "as with most hyperactive kids, I was skinny, some 10–15 pounds underweight", and considers himself to have been a target for [[Ritalin]] should it have existed at the time.<ref name="maiman18">{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-61940-8|title=The Laser Inventor|series=Springer Biographies|year=2018|isbn=978-3-319-61939-2}}</ref> In his teens Maiman earned money by repairing [[Small appliance|electric appliances]] and [[radio receiver|radio]]s,<ref name="Telegraph">{{Cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/obituaries/1551179/Theodore-Maiman.html|title=Theodore Maiman|date=May 11, 2007|publisher=The Telegraph}}</ref> and after leaving high school was employed as a junior engineer with the National Union Radio Company at age 17.<ref name="Bio">{{Cite web |url=http://www.laserinventor.com/bio.html|title=Laser Inventor, Biography of Theodore Maiman from laserinventor.com|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref>

Following a year's service in the [[United States Navy]] at the end of [[World War II]],<ref name="Waters">{{Cite book|first=Rod |last=Waters|title=Maiman Invention of the Laser: How Science Fiction Became Reality|publisher=CreateSpace Independent Publishing|year=2013|url=http://www.maimanbook.com|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref> he earned a B.S. in [[engineering physics]] from the [[University of Colorado Boulder]]. Maiman then went on to graduate studies at [[Stanford University]] where he earned an M.S. in electrical engineering in 1951 and a PhD in [[physics]] in 1955.

Maiman's doctoral thesis in [[experimental physics]], under the direction of physicist [[Willis Lamb]],<ref name="Martin" /> involved detailed microwave-optical measurements of fine structural splittings in excited helium atoms. He also devised laboratory instrumentation for Lamb's experiments. Maiman published two articles jointly with Lamb in ''[[Physical Review]]'', the second of which was based on his own thesis research.<ref>{{Cite journal|first1=T.H.|last1=Maiman|first2=W.E. Jr.|last2=Lamb|date=May 1955|title=Triplet Fine Structure of Helium|journal=Physical Review|volume=98|number=4|page=1194|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.98.1144|bibcode= 1955PhRv...98.1144.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|first1=W.E. Jr.|last1=Lamb|first2=T.H.|last2=Maiman|date=January 15, 1957|title=Measurement of the Fine Structure Separation 3<sup>3</sup>3P<sub>1</sub> – 3<sup>3</sup>P<sub>2</sub> for the Helium Atom|journal=Physical Review|volume=105|number=2|pages=573–79|doi=10.1103/physrev.105.573|bibcode=1957PhRv..105..573L}}</ref> His thesis experiment was instrumental in his development of the laser.<ref name="MaimanS" />{{Rp|43}}

==Career==
In 1956 Maiman started work with the Atomic Physics Department of the Hughes Aircraft Company (later Hughes Research Laboratories or [[HRL Laboratories]]) in California where he led the ruby [[maser]] redesign project for the [[U.S. Army Signal Corps]], reducing it from a 2.5-ton cryogenic device to {{Convert|4|lb}} while improving its performance.<ref name="Hecht" />{{Rp|88}}<ref name="Hecht2">{{Cite web|title=Oral History Transcript – Dr. Irnee D'Haenens – Interview|first=Joan|last=Bromberg|date=February 5, 1985|publisher=American Institute of Physics, Niels Bohr Library & Archives|url=http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/5015.html|access-date=December 31, 2013|archive-date=January 12, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150112061756/http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/5015.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> As a result of this success Maiman persuaded Hughes management to use company funds to support his laser project beginning in mid-1959. On a total budget of $50,000, Maiman turned to the development of a laser based on his own design with a [[Ruby#Synthesis and imitation|synthetic ruby]] crystal, which other scientists seeking to make a laser felt would not work.<ref name=gfs>{{Cite journal|first=George F.|last=Smith|date=June 1984|title=The Early Laser Years at Hughes Aircraft Company|journal=IEEE Journal of Quantum Electronics |volume=QE-20|issue=6|pages=577–84|others=excerpted as "Maiman's Work" HRL Laboratories|url=http://www.hrl.com/lasers/pdfs/maiman_work.pdf|access-date=December 2, 2015|bibcode=1984IJQE...20..577S|doi=10.1109/JQE.1984.1072445}}</ref><ref name=maiman85>Maiman, Theodore H. (1985). "The First Laser". ''Laser Pioneer Interviews''. High Tech Publications. pp. 85–99. {{ISBN|9780936551005}}</ref><ref name=oakes09>{{Cite book|chapter=Theodore Maiman|title=A to Z of STS Scientists|author=Oakes, Elizabeth H.|year=2009|page=189|publisher=Infobase |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1YDrMFug17cC&pg=PA189|isbn=978-1-4381-0925-1}}</ref>

[[File:Theodore Maiman 1960.jpg|thumb|left|Maiman with his laser in July 1960]]
On May 16, 1960, at Hughes' [[Malibu, California]], laboratories, Maiman's solid-state pink ruby laser emitted mankind's first [[Coherence (physics)|coherent light]], with rays all the same wavelength and fully in phase.<ref name="Telegraph" /> Maiman documented his invention in ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]''<ref name="Martin" /><ref name="Bio" /><ref name="Maiman2">{{Cite journal|author=Maiman, Theodore|title=Stimulated Optical Radiation in Ruby|url=http://laserfest.org/lasers/history/paper-maiman.pdf|journal=Nature|date=August 6, 1960|volume=187|issue=4736|pages=493–94|doi=10.1038/187493a0|bibcode=1960Natur.187..493M|s2cid=4224209}}</ref> on August 6, 1960, after two rejections by [[Samuel A. Goudsmit]] at ''[[Physical Review Letters]]'',<ref name=maiman18/> besides which he published other scholarly articles describing the science and technology underlying his laser.<ref name="Maiman3">{{Cite journal|first=T.H.|last=Maiman|date=June 1, 1960|title=Optical and Microwave-Optical Experiments in Ruby|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=4|issue=11|pages=564–66|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.4.564|bibcode=1960PhRvL...4..564M}}</ref><ref name="Maiman2" /><ref name="Maiman6">{{Cite journal|first=T.H.|last=Maiman|date=August 15, 1961|title=Stimulated Optical Emission in Fluorescent Solids I: Theoretical Considerations|journal=Physical Review|volume=123|issue=4|pages=1145–1150|doi=10.1103/physrev.123.1145|bibcode=1961PhRv..123.1145M}}</ref><ref name="Hoskins">{{Cite journal|author1=Maiman, T.H. |author2=Hoskins, R.H. |author3=D'Haenens, I.J. |author4=Asawa, C.K. |author5=Evtuhov, V. |name-list-style=amp |date=August 15, 1961|title=Stimulated Optical Emission in Fluorescent Solids II: Spectroscopy and Stimulated Emission in Ruby|journal=Physical Review|volume=123|issue=4|pages=1151–1157|doi=10.1103/physrev.123.1151|bibcode=1961PhRv..123.1151M}}</ref>

Maiman had begun conceptualizing a solid-state laser design even before he undertook the maser project at Hughes.<ref name="Hecht" />{{Rp|45}}<ref name="MaimanS" />{{Rp|59}} Moving the microwave frequency of masers up the electromagnetic spectrum 50,000-fold to the [[Frequency#Light|frequency of light]] would require finding a feasible lasing medium and [[Excited state|excitation]] source and designing the system.<ref name="Hecht" />{{Rp|34–37}}<ref name="Lengyel2">{{Cite book|title=Lasers|edition=2nd|publisher=Wiley-Interscience|last=Lengyel|first=Bela A.|year=1971|isbn=978-0-471-52620-9|pages=41–42}}</ref> Other major research groups at [[IBM]], [[Bell Labs]], [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]], [[Westinghouse Electric Company|Westinghouse]], [[RCA Corporation|RCA]] and [[Columbia University]], among others, were also pursuing projects to develop a laser.<ref name="Hecht" />{{Rp|7}}<ref name="MaimanS" />{{Rp|78}}

[[File:World's first laser out of case.jpg|thumb|left|World's first laser]]
Their work was stimulated by a 1958 paper by [[Arthur Leonard Schawlow|Arthur L. Schawlow]] and [[Charles H. Townes]] offering theoretical analysis and a proposal for a gaseous system using potassium vapor excited by a potassium lamp.<ref name="Bertolotti" />{{Rp|216}}<ref name="Hecht" />{{Rp|92}}<ref name="Schawlow">{{Cite journal|last1=Schawlow|first1=A.L.|last2=Townes|first2=C.H.|date=December 1958|title=Infrared and Optical Masers|journal=Physical Review|volume=112|issue=6|pages=1940–1949|doi=10.1103/physrev.112.1940|bibcode=1958PhRv..112.1940S|doi-access=free}}</ref> However Maiman identified multiple flaws in the Schawlow-Townes proposal and the reason for their rejection of a solid-state design, including a significant difference in the [[band-gap]] nature of pink rubies and red rubies, and pursued his own vision:<ref name="Hecht" />{{Rp|111}}<ref name="MaimanS" />{{Rp|159–164}}<ref name="Haenens">{{Cite journal|first=I.J.|last=D'Haenens|date=October 2007|title=Obituary: Theodore Harold Maiman|journal=Physics Today|volume=60|issue=10|page=72|doi=10.1063/1.2800106|bibcode=2007PhT....60j..72D|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=maiman18/> "I was the only one that analyzed ruby in enough detail to have the confidence to stick with it." His successful design used synthetic pink ruby crystal grown by the Linde Division of [[Union Carbide]]<ref name=maiman18/> as the [[active laser medium]] and a helical [[xenon]] flash lamp as the excitation source.<ref name="Bertolotti" />{{Rp|226–234}}<ref name="Hecht" />{{Rp|170–182}}<ref name="Lengyel3">{{Cite book|last=Lengyel|first=Bela A.|year=1966|title=Introduction to Laser Physics|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|pages=90–101}}</ref> As Townes later wrote, "Maiman's laser had several aspects not considered in our theoretical paper, nor discussed by others before the ruby demonstration."<ref name="Townes" />{{Rp|108}} One piece of evidence that convinced Maiman (and later the world) that he had lased pink ruby was that "when the crystal was pushed above threshold, we observed a brightness ratio" of the twin red lines "of more than 50 times".<ref name=maiman18/>

Following his invention of the laser, in 1961 Maiman departed Hughes to join the newly formed Quantatron company, which grew in-house ruby crystals for lasers.{{citation needed|date=April 2021}} Maiman was installed as vice president of the Applied Physics Laboratory, and he hired seven Hughes colleagues.<ref name=maiman18/>  Together they started a [[Verneuil plant]] to grow synthetic rubies, which were domestically available at that time only at Linde, who had been chosen by the US government to receive the WW2 technology transferred from Switzerland. "The Swiss for many years used this Verneuil technology to make the [[jewel bearings]] in their famous precision watches." Brothers Rick and Tony Pastor were hired by Maiman from Hughes in order to start the Quantatron synthetic ruby plant. Rick devised methods to make ultra-high purity powder, while Tony improved the burner and powder handling process.<ref name=maiman18/>

[[File:6 Maiman Laser Ruby Crystal.jpg|thumb|left|One of Maiman's original synthetic ruby lasers, dimension 9x18mm<ref name=maiman18/>]]
By 1962, when [[Louis Smullin|Smullin]] and [[Fiocco]] had already bounced the beam from a 50J 0.5 millisecond ruby laser off the moon, and the Soviets too,<ref name="smullin62">{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/1941267a0|title=Optical Echoes from the Moon|year=1962|last1=Smullin|first1=Louis D.|last2=Fiocco|first2=Giorgio|journal=Nature|volume=194|issue=4835|page=1267|bibcode=1962Natur.194.1267S|s2cid=4145783|doi-access=free}}</ref> Maiman had hired 35 people for his APL lab at Quantatron. When its funds dried up because the venture capitalist was taken over, Maiman found an eager partner in Union Carbide with whom to nurse his improved synthetic ruby plant,<ref name=maiman18/> and in 1962 Maiman founded and became the president of the Korad Corporation, which manufactured high-power ruby lasers.<ref name="Martin" /><ref name="Waters" /> Among other developments while he was at Korad, Maiman supported [[Robert W. Hellwarth]] in his [[Q-switch]] patent litigation against Gould.<ref name=maiman18/> After Korad was fully acquired by Union Carbide in 1968,<ref name="Telegraph" /> when they exercised the option written into the venture capital contract,<ref name=maiman18/> Maiman left to found Maiman Associates, a venture capital firm of his own.

Maiman was awarded US Patent Number 3,353,115 for his "Ruby Laser Systems" on November 14, 1967, and paid $300 for it by assignee Hughes Aircraft Company. It turned out to be Hughes' most profitable patent.<ref name=maiman18/>

In 1971 Maiman founded the Laser Video Corporation, and from 1976 to 1983 he worked as vice president for advanced technology at [[TRW Inc.|TRW Electronics]] (now [[Northrop Grumman]]).<ref name="Bertolotti" />{{Rp|232}} He later served as consultant to Laser Centers of America, Inc. (now [[LCA-Vision]] Inc.) and director of Control Laser Corporation. Maiman continued his involvement in laser developments and applications. In addition to his patent for the first working laser, Maiman authored a number of patents on masers, lasers, laser displays, optical scanning, and modulation.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Laser Pioneer Ted Maiman Dies at 79|publisher=LaserFocusWorld|date=May 15, 2007|url=http://www.laserfocusworld.com/articles/oer/print/volume-14/issue-10/features/laser-pioneer-ted-maiman-dies-at-79.html|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref>

Prior to his death, Maiman held an adjunct professor position in the School of Engineering Science at [[Simon Fraser University]], where he worked on the development of curricula in biophotonics, photonics and optical engineering.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sfu.ca/sfunews/stories/2019/05/moon-measurer--laser-inventor-remembered-at-international-day-of.html|title = Moon-measurer, laser inventor remembered at International Day of Light – SFU News – Simon Fraser University}}</ref>

==Awards and recognition==
Maiman received numerous prizes, awards, and accolades over the years for his development of the first laser. He was granted membership in both the [[National Academy of Sciences|National Academies of Sciences]] and [[National Academy of Engineering|Engineering]].<ref name="Hecht2" /> He was made a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], the [[The Optical Society|Optical Society of America]] (OSA), and the [[SPIE|Society of Photo-Optical Instrumentation Engineers]] (SPIE).<ref name="Bio" /> In 1962 Maiman was awarded the [[Franklin Institute]]'s [[Stuart Ballantine Medal]] for physics.<ref name="Day">{{Cite book|title=Biographical Dictionary of the History of Technology|editor1=Lance Day |editor2=Ian McNeil|year=1996|page=796|isbn=978-1-134-65020-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=m8TsygLyfSMC|last1=Day|first1=Lance|last2=McNeil|first2=Ian|publisher=Routledge }}</ref>

In 1966 Maiman received the [[American Physical Society]]'s [[Oliver E. Buckley Condensed Matter Prize]] and the [[Hertz Foundation|Fannie and John Hertz Foundation]] Award for distinguished contribution in the field of science,<ref name="Day" /> presented in a White House ceremony by President [[Lyndon B. Johnson]].<ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/ws/index.php?pid=27564|others=Online by Gerhard Peters and John T. Woolley|author=Lyndon B. Johnson|title=Remarks on Presenting the Fannie and John Hertz Foundation Award to Dr. All Javan and Dr. Theodore H. Maiman|date=April 27, 1966|journal=The American Presidency Project|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref>

[[File:Crown Prince Akihito congratulates Theodore Maiman Japan Prize 1987.jpg|thumb|Theodore Maiman at the 1987 Japan Prize award ceremony. Achievement: Realization of the world's first laser. ]]
In 1976, Maiman was awarded the Optical Society of America's [[Robert W. Wood|R.W. Wood Prize]] for "Pioneer Development of the First Laser". In 1980, he received the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]].<ref>{{cite web|title= Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref> He was the recipient of the 1983/84 [[Wolf Prize in Physics]]<ref name="Telegraph" /> and was also inducted into the [[National Inventors Hall of Fame]] that year.<ref name="Martin" /><ref>{{Cite web|publisher=National Inventors Hall of Fame|title=Inventor Profile: Theodore Harold Maiman|url=http://www.invent.org/hall_of_fame/96.html|access-date=December 31, 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140107114616/http://www.invent.org/hall_of_fame/96.html|archive-date=January 7, 2014}}</ref> In 1987 Maiman was awarded the [[Japan Prize]]<ref name="Telegraph" /> in Electro-Optics for "realization of the world's first laser."<ref>{{Cite web|publisher=The Japan Prize Foundation|title=Laureates|url=http://www.japanprize.jp/en/laureates_by_nameK-O.html|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref>

In 1994, he was inducted as an honorary fellow of the [[Royal College of Surgeons of England]], the only non-physician, non-royal member. Time magazine cited Maiman's invention of the laser as among the twenty most important technological developments of the 20th century.<ref name="Technology">{{Cite web|url=https://content.time.com/time/photogallery/0,29307,2026224_2200997,00.html|title=20th Century Technology|work=TIME.com |access-date=February 2, 2015|publisher=Time}}</ref> Many universities granted Maiman honorary degrees, with the last from [[Simon Fraser University]] in 2002.<ref name="IEEE">{{Cite web|url=http://www.ieeeghn.org/wiki/index.php/Milestones:List_of_IEEE_Milestones|title=List of IEEE Milestones|website=IEEE Global History Network|publisher=IEEE|access-date=August 3, 2011}}</ref>

Recognition for Maiman and his laser invention continued posthumously. In a 2007 obituary testimonial, maser co-inventor [[Charles H. Townes]] described Maiman's 1960 ''Nature'' article on his laser as "probably more important per word than any of the papers published by Nature over the past century."<ref>{{Cite journal|first=Charles H.|last=Townes|date=June 7, 2007|title=Obituary: Theodore H. Maiman (1927–2007), Maker of the First Laser |journal=Nature|volume=447|issue=7145|page=654|doi=10.1038/447654a|pmid=17554298|bibcode=2007Natur.447..654G|s2cid=4388584|doi-access=free}}</ref> The annual Theodore Maiman Student Paper Competition was established in 2008, endowed by major laser groups, and is administered by the OSA Foundation.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Maiman Student Paper Competition|publisher=OSA|url=http://www.osa.org/en-us/foundation/student_funding/maiman_student_paper_competition|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref> In 2010 numerous events were staged worldwide by major scientific and industry photonics organizations to celebrate the 50th anniversary of Maiman's first laser and subsequent lasers under the umbrella of LaserFest.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.laserfest.org|title=LaserFest: Celebrating 50 Years of Laser Innovation|access-date=December 2, 2015}}</ref>

The U.S. Congress passed a resolution celebrating the invention of the laser and citing Maiman.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Recognizing the 50th Anniversary of the Laser|website=House Resolution 1310, 111th Congress|url=https://www.govtrack.us/congress/bills/111/hres1310/text|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref> Also in 2010 Maiman's laser achievement was recognized as an [[List of IEEE milestones|IEEE Milestone]],<ref name="IEEE" /> and the American Physical Society presented Hughes Research Laboratories with a plaque to commemorate the historic site of the world's first laser.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Theodore Maiman: Hughes Research Laboratories, Malibu, California|publisher=APS Historic Sites|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/outreach/history/historicsites/maiman.cfm|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref>

In 2011, Maiman was recognized by [[Stanford University]] as a "Stanford Engineering Hero", citing his "rare blend of advanced training in physics and engineering combined with significant laboratory experience".<ref>{{Cite web|title=2011 Stanford Engineering Heroes|publisher=Stanford University|url=http://engineering.stanford.edu/2011-stanford-engineering-heroes|access-date=December 31, 2013|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140107114943/http://engineering.stanford.edu/2011-stanford-engineering-heroes|archive-date=January 7, 2014}}</ref> In 2014, the National Academy of Sciences published a biographical memoir of Maiman including a tribute by [[Nick Holonyak|Nick Holonyak, Jr.]]<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/maiman-theodore.pdf|author=Andrew H. Rawicz|title=Theodore H. Maiman (1927–2007)|date=2014|pages=23–31|access-date=February 2, 2015|journal=National Academy of Sciences}}</ref>

In 2017 [[UNESCO]] declared May 16 the [[International Day of Light]], which is celebrated every year by numerous laser and light-related events around the world.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.lightday.org|title=International Day of Light|access-date=July 8, 2020}}</ref> That date commemorates Maiman's first successful firing of his laser.

==Death==
Maiman died from [[Mastocytosis|systemic mastocytosis]] on May 5, 2007, in [[Vancouver]], British Columbia, Canada, where he lived with his second wife, Kathleen,<ref name="Martin">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/05/11/obituaries/11maiman.html?_r=0|title=Theodore Maiman, 79, Dies; Demonstrated First Laser|last=Martin|first=Douglas|date=May 11, 2007|work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|first=Doris|last=Kilbane|date=December 7, 2009|title=Theodore Maiman: Professional Focus, Personal Warmth|publisher=Electronic Design|url=http://electronicdesign.com/analog/theodore-maiman-professional-focus-personal-warmth|access-date=December 31, 2013}}</ref> whom he met on February 13, 1984. He had one daughter, named Sheri, with his first wife, Shirley, whom he married in 1956. Sheri Maiman died of cancer in 1988 at the age of 30.<ref name=maiman18/>
